findings.title: extend_query_with silently drops existing query parameters with blank values
findings.property: extending a query keeps all existing key/value pairs, including those with empty values, and appends the new ones
findings.actual: query == 'b=c' (the existing 'a=' is lost); extending with [] turns 'a=' into ''
findings.evidence: Docstring: 'Extend the existing query string with the new query items.' Existing items are parsed with parse_qsl(self.query) without keep_blank_values=True, so blank-valued params are discarded; extension should only add, never remove.

    a=[(
         '0',  # or any other generated value
         '',
     )],
    b=[],  # or any other generated value
)

review.title: URIBuilder.extend_query_with drops existing query parameters that have blank values
review.reason: extend_query_with parses the existing query with `parse_qsl(self.query or "")`. That call defaults to `keep_blank_values=False`, so `a=` is discarded, and extending with an empty list turns `a=` into an empty query. The docstring says it extends the existing query, and the examples show existing items being preserved. Losing data from a query that was already valid is not the intended behaviour. The tests I found don't cover blank values, so nothing suggests the drop is deliberate, and passing `keep_blank_values=True` is a one-line fix a maintainer would likely accept.

findings.reproSource:
from rfc3986.builder import URIBuilder


def test_repro_extend_query_blank():
    b = URIBuilder(query="a=").extend_query_with([("b", "c")])
    assert b.query == "a=&b=c"

findings.title: ParseResultBytes.unsplit() crashes for any URI without an authority
findings.property: unsplitting a parsed relative/authority-less URI (bytes) returns the URI bytes instead of raising
findings.actual: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'encode' raised in ParseResultBytes.authority (parseresult.py:409), because reference.authority is None
findings.evidence: unsplit is documented as ':returns: The parsed URI reconstituted as a string / :rtype: bytes'; the str counterpart ParseResult.unsplit and geturl() work for the same input, and authority-less URIs such as '/a', 'a:b', '?q' and '' are valid RFC 3986 references that from_string accepts. ParseResultMixin declares authority as Optional.

Failing test case: test_bytes_unsplit_vs_str(
    u='',
    lazy=True,
)

review.title: ParseResultBytes.unsplit() raises AttributeError for URIs without an authority
review.reason: I re-ran the repro and it fails as reported. `ParseResultBytes.authority` (parseresult.py:409) calls `self.reference.authority.encode(...)` with no None check, although `ParseResult.authority` and the mixin both declare the value Optional. `from_string` accepts authority-less references such as b'/a', and the str `unsplit` handles them. The default `lazy_normalize=True` path in `ParseResultBytes.unsplit` hits the crash on a plain relative path, which is a common input, so a maintainer would accept a small None-guard fix.

findings.reproSource:
from rfc3986.parseresult import ParseResultBytes


def test_repro_bytes_unsplit_no_authority():
    pr = ParseResultBytes.from_string(b"/a")
    assert pr.unsplit() == b"/a"

findings.title: normalize_uri drops an empty authority (file:///x -> file:/x)
findings.property: normalizing a URI preserves its component structure; an empty-but-present authority stays '//'
findings.evidence: RFC 3986 section 5.3 recomposition: if authority is defined (even empty), append '//' + authority. Docstring says normalize_uri equals uri_reference(uri).normalize().unsplit(); normalization (6.2.2) must not change the URI's meaning. unsplit() uses truthiness of authority, so '//' is lost (also '//' -> '').

review.title: normalize_uri drops an empty-but-present authority (file:///path becomes file:/path)
review.reason: normalize() rebuilds the authority with normalize_authority(), which returns '' for an empty authority. unsplit() then tests `if self.authority:`, so the '//' is dropped, and `file:///etc/hosts` becomes `file:/etc/hosts`. RFC 3986 5.3 says '//' is emitted whenever the authority is defined, even if empty, and normalization shouldn't change a URI's structure. I read the source and found no test or documentation saying the drop is intended. I could not run the code (Bash was denied), so this rests on reading the source and the counterhound run, which failed 3/3. The fix is delicate because it has to tell None from '' for authority across parsing, normalization and unsplit, which is why I'm only moderately confident a maintainer would take it.

findings.reproSource:
from rfc3986.api import normalize_uri


def test_repro_empty_authority_dropped():
    # "file:///etc/hosts" has an empty (but present) authority; normalizing
    # must not change the URI's structure.
    assert normalize_uri("file:///etc/hosts") == "file:///etc/hosts"

findings.title: normalize_uri turns a '//'-leading path into an authority
findings.property: normalized URI re-parses with the same authority presence as the input
findings.expected: a path of '//b' with no authority (e.g. 'a:/.//b' or 'a:/%2F...' style form); result must not re-parse with authority 'b'
findings.actual: 'a://b', which parses as scheme 'a', authority 'b', no path
findings.evidence: RFC 3986 section 3.3: when no authority is present the path cannot begin with '//'; section 6.2.2 normalization must be semantics-preserving. remove_dot_segments produces '//b' and unsplit() concatenates it directly after 'a:'.

review.title: normalize_uri turns a path beginning with '//' into an authority when the URI has no authority
review.reason: 'a:/.//b' is a valid URI: scheme 'a', no authority, path '/.//b'. Normalization runs remove_dot_segments to get '//b', and unsplit() then emits 'a:' followed by '//b'. That string re-parses with authority 'b' and no path, so normalization changed the URI's meaning, which RFC 3986 §6.2 forbids and §3.3 rules out for a no-authority path. This is a narrow edge case, and a fix is small: when there is no authority and the path starts with '//', keep a '/.' prefix as the WHATWG URL spec does, or skip dot-segment removal that would create the leading '//'. I couldn't run the repro myself because shell access was denied, so this rests on reading the source and on the harness's three failing runs.

findings.reproSource:
from rfc3986.api import normalize_uri, uri_reference


def test_repro_path_becomes_authority():
    # path "/.//b" normalizes to "//b"; with no authority the result
    # "a://b" re-parses with host "b" instead of path "//b".
    n = normalize_uri("a:/.//b")
    assert uri_reference(n).authority is None
